summary: Gives guidance to people designing new DHCPv6 options so that the formats are easy for existing DHCPv6 software to adopt. It also gives guidelines for expert reviewers who evaluate new option registrations. It updates RFC 3315.

plainLanguage.summary: This document tells the people who design new DHCPv6 options how to write them so that the software already deployed in networks can handle them without changes. It is a checklist of design choices that make options easy to adopt.

subtitle: A how-to for designing new DHCPv6 options so that existing software can carry them without changes.

tldr.problem: A new DHCPv6 option can be correct on the wire and still be hard to deploy. If it needs new code, a new configuration file format or special handling, it will meet resistance from the software already running in the field.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7227 gives designers a checklist: reuse existing option formats, avoid conditional formats and aliasing, choose between a name and an address deliberately, state whether an option may appear more than once, and write separate client, server and relay behaviour sections.
tldr.outcome: The result is guidance for anyone writing a new option and for the expert reviewers who judge such proposals. It is a Best Current Practice from May 2014 that updates RFC 3315 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7227 is a Best Current Practice published in May 2014. It updates RFC 3315, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: Options That Nobody Deploys
sections.content:
Most protocol developers ask themselves if a protocol will work, or work efficiently. Another less frequently considered question is whether the proposed protocol presents itself needless barriers to adoption by deployed software. DHCPv6 software implementors are not merely faced with the task of handling a given option's format on the wire: the option must fit into every stage of the system's process, starting with the user interface used to enter the configuration up to the machine interfaces where configuration is ultimately consumed.

Another frequently overlooked aspect of rapid adoption is whether the option requires operators to be intimately familiar with the option's internal format in order to use it. Most DHCPv6 software provides a facility for handling unknown options at the time of publication, and the handling of such options usually needs to be manually configured by the operator. If doing so requires extensive reading, it inhibits adoption.

Although a given solution would work, and might even be space, time or aesthetically optimal, an option is presented with a series of ever-worsening challenges to be adopted. It may not fit neatly into existing configuration files. It may require source code changes to be adopted and hence upgrades of deployed software. It may not share its deployment fate in a general manner with other options, standing alone in requiring code changes or reworking configuration file syntaxes. And it may work well in the deployment environment its proponents currently envision while failing or producing inconsistent results in some other equally valid environment.
sections.plainLanguage: A new option only helps if the software already in the field can carry it. If it needs a new code path or a new file format, it will not be adopted, however good it is.

sections.title: The Guiding Principle: Reuse
sections.content:
The primary guiding principle to follow in order to enhance an option's adoptability is reuse. The option should be created in such a way that does not require any new or special case software to support. If old software that is currently deployed and in the field can adopt the option through supplied configuration facilities, then it is fairly certain that new software can formally adopt it easily.

There are at least two classes of DHCPv6 options. Simple options are provided explicitly to carry data from one side of the DHCPv6 exchange to the other, such as name servers, domain names or time servers. Protocol class options require special processing on the part of the DHCPv6 software or are used during special processing, such as the Fully Qualified Domain Name option; these carry data that is the result of a routine in some DHCPv6 software. The guidelines should be applied in a relaxed manner for the protocol class of options, since wherever a special case code is already required, it is substantially more reasonable to format the option in a less generic fashion if there are measurable benefits to doing so.

The easiest approach to manufacturing trivially deployable options is to assemble the option out of whatever common fragments fit, possibly allowing a group of data elements to repeat to fill the remaining space and thus provide multiple values. Fixed-size values go at the start of the option and variable or indeterminate-sized values at the tail end. Implementations will then likely be able to reuse code paths designed to support other options. There is a trade-off between adoptability and the advantages that new formats can provide, but in general it is usually preferable to reuse previously used option formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Build the new option out of pieces that already exist: a list of addresses, a number, a name, a flag. Software that already handles those pieces handles the new option for free.

sections.title: The Common Option Formats
sections.content:
The RFC lists a set of common option format data elements as shorthand, though the list is not complete.

An option with IPv6 addresses carries one or many IPv6 addresses, sometimes limited to one, and is used by options such as the DHCPv6 server unicast address, the SIP servers address list, DNS recursive name servers and the NIS, SNTP and NTP server addresses. An option with a single flag, or boolean, is defined with no content at all: the presence or absence of the option conveys the value. The absence represents the default value and the presence the other value, which does not necessarily mean that absence is off and presence is on; if the default is on, the name should reflect that, for example OPTION_DISABLE_FOO.

An option with an IPv6 prefix carries the 128-bit prefix together with a length from 0 to 128. Because /64 or shorter prefixes are common, most of the prefix data would be zeros and unused, so the prefix is stored in the variable-length data field instead: one octet holds prefix6len and the prefix field is (prefix6len + 7) / 8 octets, padded with zero bits up to the nearest octet boundary. For example, the prefix 2001:db8::/60 is encoded with an option-length of 9, prefix6len of 60 and eight octets containing 20 01 0d b8 00 00 00 00. The IAPREFIX option defined by RFC 3633 uses a full-length 16-octet prefix field, because the concern about option length was not well understood at the time of its publication.

The remaining formats are a 32-bit signed or unsigned integer value, a 16-bit integer value, an 8-bit integer value, a URI, a text string, variable-length data and a DNS wire format domain name list. If more complex options are needed, these basic formats may be treated as primitives that can be used to build more complex formats. It is often easier to implement two options with trivial formats than one option with a more complex format, although splitting one complex option into two or more simple options can introduce inter-option dependencies that should be avoided.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives a catalogue of shapes an option can take, with an example of each. The advice is to copy one of them rather than invent a new shape, unless a new shape buys something real.

sections.title: Things to Avoid
sections.content:
Conditional formatting, where an octet at the start of the option says how to process the rest, may appear simple to the casual observer, but the only conditional formatting methods in widespread use today are protocol class options. Conditional formatting therefore requires new code to be written and complicates future interoperability should new conditional formats be added, since existing code has to ignore conditional formats it does not support.

Options are said to be aliases of each other if they provide input to the same configuration parameter. A commonly proposed example is to configure the location of a new service using a binary IP address, a domain name field and a URL. This kind of aliasing is undesirable and is not recommended. Where three different formats are supposed to be supported, it more than triples the work of the software involved, requiring support not merely for one format but for producing and digesting all three, and code development and testing must cover all possible combinations of defined formats. Since clients cannot predict what the server will provide, they must request all formats, so when the server is configured with all formats the DHCPv6 message bandwidth is wasted on redundant contents, and the option number space is wasted, as three new option codes are required rather than one.

It also becomes unclear which types of values are mandatory and how configuring some of the options may influence the others. If an operator configures only the URL, should the server synthesize a domain name and an IP address? A single configuration value on a host is probably presented to the operator, or other software on the machine, in a single field or channel; if that channel has a natural format, then any alternative formats merely make more work for intervening software in providing conversions. The best advice is to choose the one method that best fulfils the requirements for simplicity, such as an IP address and a port pair, for late binding, such as with DNS, or for completeness, such as with a URL.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things cause trouble: an option whose shape changes depending on a byte at the front, and offering the same setting in several different formats at once. Both multiply the work for every implementation.

sections.title: Choosing a Name or an Address
sections.content:
Some parameters may be specified as an FQDN or an address. In most cases one or the other should be used, and it is strongly discouraged to define both option types at the same time unless there is sufficient motivation to do so.

There is no single recommendation that works for every case. For parameters that are network specific or represent aspects of network infrastructure, like available mobility services, addresses are usually the more usable choice. For parameters that are application-specific configuration, like SIP servers, an FQDN is usually better, because applications are often better suited to deal with FQDN failures than with address failures: most operating systems provide a way to retry an FQDN resolution, while there is typically no API for applications to reconfigure over DHCP to get a new address value.

An FQDN imposes a number of additional failure modes: the client must know about available DNS servers, so the DNS servers option becomes mandatory and this should be mentioned in the document; the DNS may not be reachable; the DNS may be available but have no appropriate information, such as no AAAA records; the address family must be specified and the record may be of another type; it must be decided what to do with multiple records; multihomed devices may be connected to different administrative domains with different DNS answers; and it should be said whether Internationalized Domain Names are allowed.

Addresses are easier to implement, have trivial validation, are explicit, allow no ambiguity, are faster because they need no extra round trip, and do not require the client to implement DNS resolution. A name does offer one thing an address cannot: it lets a change in DNS be picked up by clients, which is only useful when the resolution is done by the client when the content of the option is actually consumed.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is simpler and works offline; a name can change without the server sending anything new, but the client then needs a working DNS setup. Pick one, and the RFC says which to pick for network settings and which for application settings.

sections.title: Size, Repetition and Order
sections.content:
DHCPv6 allows for packet sizes up to 64 KB. It is feasible to suggest that DHCPv6 is capable of having larger options deployed over it, and at least no common upper limit is yet known to have been encoded by its implementors, so it is not really possible to describe a fixed limit that cleanly divides workable option sizes from those that are too big. It is advantageous to prefer option formats that contain the desired information in the smallest form that satisfies the requirements. It is better to split distinct values into separate octets than to propose overly complex bit-shifting operations to save several bits that would be padded to the next octet boundary anyway.

DHCPv6 does allow for multiple instances of a given option, treated as distinct values following the defined format, but this feature is generally preferred to be restricted to protocol class features such as the IA_ series of options. In such cases it is better to define an option as an array if it is possible. It is recommended to clarify with normative language whether a given option may appear once or multiple times; the default assumption is only once.

Documents that define new options SHOULD state whether or not these options are singletons. Unless otherwise specified, newly defined options are considered to be singletons, and if multiple instances are allowed the document MUST explain how to use them. Allowing multiple instances often leads to confusion: during the standardization of DS-Lite there was a discussion of whether multiple instances of the tunnel option should be allowed, which created an unfounded expectation that clients would do failover or load balancing between the endpoints provided. Neither was defined, so it caused confusion, and it was eventually decided to allow only one instance.

Option order, either among many options or among multiple instances of the same option, SHOULD NOT be significant, and new documents MUST NOT assume any specific option processing order. Since RFC 3315 does not impose option order, some implementations use hash tables to store received options, which is conformant, and depending on the hash implementation the processing order is almost always different from the order on the wire. An option definition SHOULD instead restrict ordering by using a single option that contains ordered fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Say how many times an option may appear, and do not rely on the order options arrive in. Software is free to store them in a hash table, which scrambles the order.

sections.title: Keeping the Server Simple
sections.content:
DHCP is designed for provisioning clients. Less experienced protocol designers often assume that it is easy to define an option that will convey a different parameter for each client in a network. Such problems arose during the designs of MAP and 4rd. While it would be easier for provisioned clients to get ready to use per-client option values, such a requirement puts exceedingly large loads on the server side, may introduce new implementation complexity and additional database state on the server, and alternatives should be considered if possible. As an example, MAP was designed so that all clients are provisioned with the same set of MAP options, and each provisioned client uses its unique address and delegated prefix to generate client-specific information, which introduces no additional state for the server and therefore scales better.

Contrary to DHCPv4, DHCPv6 keeps several timers for renewals. Each IA_NA and IA_PD contains T1 and T2 timers that designate the time after which the client will initiate renewal, and those timers apply only to their associated IA containers. Refreshing other parameters should be initiated after a time specified in the information refresh time option. Introducing additional timers makes deployment unnecessarily complex and SHOULD be avoided.

In general, DHCPv6 clients only refresh configuration data from the server when the T1 timer expires, and although there is a Reconfigure mechanism, support for it is optional and cannot be relied upon. Even when clients refresh, not all consumers notice the changes: a server started with parameters from an early transaction may keep using them indefinitely. When designing an option, take into account the fact that it may hold stale data that will only be updated at an arbitrary time in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not design an option that needs a different value for every client, and do not add new timers. The server should stay simple, and the option's value may be stale for a long time anyway.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DHCPv6 does have an authentication mechanism that makes it possible for software to discriminate between authentic endpoints and man-in-the-middle. Other authentication mechanisms may optionally be deployed. Sadly, as of 2014 the authentication in DHCPv6 is rarely used and support for it is not common in existing implementations. Some specific deployment types make it mandatory, so in certain cases specific authentication aspects can be relied upon, but that is not true in the generic case.

So, while creating a new option, it is prudent to assume that the DHCPv6 packet contents are always transmitted in the clear, and actual production use will probably be vulnerable at least to man-in-the-middle attacks from within the network. In particular, some DHCPv6 message exchanges are transmitted to multicast addresses that are likely broadcast anyway.

If an option is of a specific fixed length, it is useful to remind the implementor of the option data's full length by declaring the specific value of the length tag, which helps remind implementors to validate the option length before digesting it into fixed-length regions of memory or stack. If an option may be of variable size, it is advisable to either define a reasonable upper limit and suggest validating it, or explicitly remind the implementor that an option may be exceptionally long. For some option contents, out-of-bound values may be used to breach security: an IP address field might carry a loopback or local multicast address, and a domain name field might be filled with contrived contents that exceed the limitations on domain name formatting and are then implicitly trusted. Authors are therefore strongly advised to define validation measures that recipients must perform before processing such options, while referring to the base specification rather than copying its validation language.

On privacy, the DHCPv6 packets are typically transmitted in the clear and are susceptible to eavesdropping, which should be considered when defining options that may convey personally identifying information or other sensitive data. Unless the underlying transmission technology provides a secure channel, the DHCPv6 options SHOULD NOT include personally identifying information or other sensitive information. If special circumstances warrant sending such information over unsecured DHCPv6, the dangers MUST be clearly discussed in the security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Assume anyone on the network can read and rewrite the configuration. Check the values you accept, fix the length of fixed-size options, and keep personal data out of options that travel in the clear.

items.title: Conditional formatting
items.text: A leading byte that changes how the rest is read needs new code in every implementation.

items.title: Aliasing
items.text: Offering the same setting as an address, a name and a URL multiplies the work.

items.title: Extra timers
items.text: New renewal timers make deployment more complex and should be avoided.

items.title: Order dependence
items.text: Never assume options are processed in the order they arrive.
